channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Hackers reportedly reached a tanker’s navigation, propulsion and cargo systems — and the FBI has confirmed a second ship
item.description: The story that broke on Wednesday got considerably worse on Friday. The FBI and Coast Guard boarded two US-bound oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico on 21 and 24 August after both vessels’ networks showed signs of compromise; new reporting says attackers reached the navigation, propulsion and cargo systems of at least one of them. The named ship, the 333-metre VL Prosperity, was compromised on 7 August en route from Egypt to Galveston, lost communications for more than a day, and had its speed and fuel systems interfered with. The FBI has now confirmed a second Texas-bound tanker was hit. Nobody has been attributed. For OT defenders the point is blunt: a vessel is a mobile control-system site that berths against your terminal, and nobody inspects its network. - FBI and US Coast Guard joint statement, reported by TechCrunch; vessel identification and the speed, fuel and communications detail from CBS News; second-vessel confirmation from follow-up reporting - Boardings 21 and 24 Aug 2026; agencies’ joint statement 16 Sep 2026; control-system detail reported 18 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] More than a hundred water systems, one campaign, and the only thing the attackers needed was a PLC facing the internet
item.category: Incident — confirmed OT compromise of internet-exposed PLCs across more than 100 US water systems
item.description: CISA has confirmed that over 100 US water and wastewater systems were targeted during July, in a campaign federal agencies attribute to Iran-affiliated actors and characterise as opportunistic rather than selective. The technique was not sophisticated: find a programmable logic controller reachable from the public internet, change its password and its network settings, and lock the operator out of their own equipment. Some utilities reported flooding and drops in water pressure afterwards. Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers were named first; the joint advisory has since been widened to Schneider Electric and Siemens devices, with the actors also using vendors’ own engineering software — Studio 5000, EcoStruxure Control Expert, TIA Portal — to pull project files out of victim environments. This is the clearest confirmed OT-disruptive campaign in the current window, and none of it required a vulnerability. - CISA confirmation reported by TechCrunch; joint CISA, FBI, EPA and NSA advisory AA26-097A; FBI alert to the water and wastewater sector - Attacks late Jul 2026; advisory updated 22 Jul 2026; CISA confirmation of scale reported 26 Aug 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The router at the unmanned site can be taken over the SSH port without a password — and it was being taken a day before the fix shipped
item.category: Incident — confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of chained SSH flaws in edge routers
item.description: CERT Polska coordinated disclosure of six RouterOS vulnerabilities and confirmed that two of them, chained, give an unauthenticated attacker full control of any MikroTik device with SSH reachable from the internet. The chain — CVE-2026-67276, an SSH authentication bypass, with CVE-2026-86060, a session privilege manipulation flaw triggered by specially crafted usernames — is being actively exploited, with activity observed from at least 2 September, a day before MikroTik shipped patched builds. The Shadowserver Foundation counted roughly 122,500 RouterOS devices with SSH exposed in a single 24-hour scan. MikroTik gear is not an OT product, which is exactly the problem: it is the cheap, capable router that turns up at wellpads, pump stations, substations and remote skids, often installed by an integrator and never entered into an asset register. A useful indicator of compromise is an SSH user literally named “-2”. - CERT Polska advisory, with exposure counts from the Shadowserver Foundation and corroboration from Help Net Security and Industrial Cyber - Exploitation observed from 2 Sep 2026; patches 3 Sep 2026; CERT Polska disclosure 5 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] During an active support session, someone can push a file to your machine and run it — no authorisation, no prompt
item.category: Incident — confirmed exploitation of remote support software used by integrators and managed service providers
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-84869 in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 September after confirming in-the-wild attacks, with a federal remediation deadline of 14 September under BOD 26-04. The flaw — improper privilege management combined with missing authorisation, rated CVSS 9.9 — lets an attacker transfer a file to a device during an active remote session and execute it without the host user authorising or even being asked. ConnectWise patched on 8 September. ScreenConnect is the tool a very large number of system integrators, OEM service organisations and managed service providers use to reach industrial customers, which means the affected device is frequently an engineering workstation or an HMI server sitting inside a plant network, and the session is one the site itself invited. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, reported by BleepingComputer and SC Media - Patch 8 Sep 2026; KEV addition 11 Sep 2026; federal deadline 14 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] An IT compromise, no control system touched, and the plants still stopped — the clearest recent illustration of why recovery is an operations problem
item.category: Incident — confirmed IT compromise with sustained manufacturing and order-processing disruption
item.description: Boston Scientific has continued to report operational disruption following a cybersecurity incident affecting its IT systems and order processing, with manufacturing and distribution affected across sites. No compromise of process control has been reported; the mechanism is the familiar one, where the systems that schedule work, move material, release batches and record quality sit in enterprise IT, and production cannot legally or practically proceed without them. It is worth pairing with research published this month arguing that manufacturers consistently underestimate the gap between IT restoration and production restart — IT comes back in hours, capacity does not come back for days, and the difference is material staging, recertification, requalification and the simple fact that a line does not resume where it stopped. - Company disclosure reported by Industrial Cyber, with recovery-gap analysis from Industrial Cyber sector research - Disruption reported 28 Aug 2026 and continuing — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Twelve ways into a Siemens edge box, and four of them are reachable by malformed PROFINET discovery traffic
item.category: Vendor research — Nozomi Networks Labs; twelve flaws in a Siemens industrial edge device, chainable to root
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published research on the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403, a local processing engine used as an industrial edge device, identifying twelve vulnerabilities in firmware below V4.0 HF0 — privilege escalation, path traversal, authentication bypass, command injection, buffer overflows and memory-handling issues, with CVSS scores between 5.3 and 8.5. Several can be chained to obtain root. Separately, an emulation-driven fuzzing campaign against the device’s PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol implementation — built from process snapshots, the Unicorn CPU emulator and AFL++ — turned up four memory-corruption flaws, CVE-2025-40575 through CVE-2025-40578, each rated CVSS 4.0 5.3: an uninitialised value, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads. The DCP flaws matter disproportionately because DCP is unauthenticated link-layer traffic: anything on the PROFINET segment can send it. - Nozomi Networks Labs research, reported by Industrial Cyber; CVE assignments coordinated with Siemens ProductCERT - Published 16 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Manufacturing ransomware up 40% this year, and the industrial damage keeps arriving without anyone touching a control system
item.category: Threat intelligence — industrial ransomware volume and targeting, Dragos quarterly analysis and sector reporting
item.description: Dragos counted 1,140 ransomware incidents against industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up about 12% on the 1,020 recorded in the first, with manufacturing taking 747 of them — roughly 65% — and ICS-adjacent firms such as engineering houses, system integrators and equipment makers second at 117. Separate sector reporting puts the rise in attacks on manufacturers at around 40% year to date. The consistent finding is that ransomware crews do not need control-system access to stop production: the incidents cluster at the IT/OT boundary, against ERP, virtualisation infrastructure, identity services and remote access gateways, because disrupting those cascades into a shutdown faster and more reliably than anything done to a PLC. The named actor set this quarter runs Qilin, The Gentlemen, Akira, DragonForce and INC Ransom. - Dragos industrial ransomware analysis for Q2 2026, with year-to-date manufacturing figures reported by SecurityWeek - Dragos Q2 analysis published Aug 2026; year-to-date manufacturing figures reported 9 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The workforce problem is not headcount — 27% of organisations now tie a breach directly to a capability gap
item.category: Research — SANS Institute and GIAC workforce study, with critical-infrastructure and OT framing
item.description: The 2026 SANS and GIAC workforce study argues the familiar “talent shortage” framing is wrong: teams are largely in place, and what they lack is specific capability against current threats. Around 60% of organisations say their teams lack the right skills, regulatory pressure on hiring has jumped from 40% to 95% in a year, and 27% report breaches they attribute directly to those capability gaps. The OT relevance is straightforward and uncomfortable: industrial environments rarely fail because nobody is on shift, they fail because the people on shift have never configured a control-network sensor, read a PROFINET capture, or run an incident where the decision was whether to keep making product. AI is also eroding the entry-level work that used to serve as the training ground, which hits OT hardest because the apprenticeship was already informal. - SANS Institute and GIAC 2026 workforce report, with critical-infrastructure framing from Industrial Cyber - Reported 16 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The box that decides which VLAN a device lands in can be taken by an unauthenticated request — and it is being taken
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-76460, CVSS 10.0, Cisco Identity Services Engine; exploited as a zero-day, no workaround
item.description: Cisco disclosed a maximum-severity authentication bypass in Identity Services Engine and the ISE Passive Identity Connector, tracked as CVE-2026-76460 at CVSS 10.0, caused by insufficient authentication control on an API endpoint. An unauthenticated remote attacker can bypass the web management interface and gain unauthorised access to the device. Cisco says it was exploited as a zero-day; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 16 September with a federal remediation deadline of 19 September. There is no workaround — upgrading is the only remediation. For industrial sites, ISE is frequently the thing enforcing which devices land on which VLAN, including the segment boundary between enterprise and plant. Whoever holds ISE can rewrite that boundary without touching a switch, a firewall or a controller. - Cisco security advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, reported by BleepingComputer - KEV addition 16 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 19 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The block password that protects your control logic can be walked past — and patching the software alone does not fix it
item.category: Advisory — ICSA-26-260-02, CVE-2026-15688, CVSS v4 9.2, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-260-02 on 17 September covering CVE-2026-15688, an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm in Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and the Motion Control Settings software packaged with it, rated CVSS v4 9.2. All versions are affected. A local attacker who can run the engineering software and modify part of its executable module in memory can authenticate with an invalid block password and then view, tamper with, destroy or delete control programs. This is not a network authentication bypass against a PLC — it is an attack on the protection you rely on to stop a contractor, a temporary engineer or anyone with access to the engineering workstation from reading or altering protected program blocks. The awkward part is the remediation: updating the software is insufficient unless each project is also moved to security version 2. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-260-02, drawn from the Mitsubishi Electric PSIRT advisory - Published 17 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] An unauthenticated request that carries its own script — a workflow engine is being exploited a month after the proof of concept landed
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-58138, CVSS 9.8, Orkes Conductor workflow orchestration; exploited in the wild since August
item.description: Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-58138, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Orkes Conductor rated CVSS 9.8. The vulnerability is reached through inline workflow definitions submitted to the workflow API: an attacker embeds malicious JavaScript or Python expressions in a definition, and the engine evaluates them into arbitrary system commands. The timeline is a familiar one — patched in June in version 3.30.2, proof-of-concept code published in early August, in-the-wild attacks identified on 21 August, and roughly 1,300 exploitation attempts blocked by one vendor across 8–9 September alone. Conductor is not ICS software, but workflow orchestration engines increasingly sit in industrial data platforms, MES integrations and asset-management pipelines, on the enterprise side of the boundary and with credentials that reach both ways. - SecurityWeek, drawing on Empirical and Fortinet telemetry and the Orkes advisory - Patched June 2026; in-the-wild attacks from 21 Aug 2026; reported 18 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A control platform for grid compensation equipment, a component shipped since 2020, and confidentiality, integrity and availability all in scope
item.category: Advisory — ICSA-26-260-03, Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform; transmission-level reactive power compensation
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-260-03 on 17 September covering vulnerabilities in the Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform, the control system for flexible AC transmission systems equipment. The advisory scopes the issue to FACTS control systems that include the GWS component and were deployed from 2020 onwards; deployments without GWS are not affected. Successful exploitation can affect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the product. The affected product list reads like a transmission substation inventory: SVC Light (STATCOM), fixed series capacitors, thyristor-controlled series capacitors, static VAr compensators, static watt compensators and hybrid synchronous condensers. This is equipment that manages voltage stability and power flow on transmission networks, which puts it in a different consequence category from most advisories on this page. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-260-03, republished from the Hitachi Energy advisory - Published 17 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A controller and its Ethernet modules, five sectors, and a fix that has been sitting on the vendor portal
item.category: Advisory — ICSA-26-260-04, CVE-2025-6625, CVSS v3 7.5, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 and BMXNOE communication modules
item.description: CISA republished Schneider Electric’s advisory SEVD-2025-224-05 as ICSA-26-260-04 on 17 September, covering CVE-2025-6625 in the Modicon M340 controller and the BMXNOE0100 and BMXNOE0110 Ethernet communication modules, rated CVSS v3 7.5. The product sees use in chemical, commercial facilities, critical manufacturing, energy, and water and wastewater environments, globally. Fixed versions are available: BMXNOE0100 version 3.60, BMXNOE0110 version 6.80 and Modicon M340 SV3.70. The republication is worth noticing in its own right — CISA is increasingly carrying vendor CSAF advisories verbatim for visibility, which means an advisory can appear on the ICS feed months after the vendor first issued it, and the practical question for asset owners is whether the fix ever actually got applied. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-260-04, republished from Schneider Electric CPCERT advisory SEVD-2025-224-05 - Republished by CISA 17 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Seven advisories in one afternoon: a data-centre edge platform, a UPS shutdown agent, an environment monitor and an electronic logging device
item.category: Advisory batch — CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, published 17 September 2026
item.description: CISA published seven ICS advisories on 17 September, three of which are covered separately on this page. The rest: ICSA-26-260-01 for Bransys ELD, an electronic logging device used in commercial road transport; ICSA-26-260-05 for Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 models 750 and 755, the environment monitoring appliances that watch temperature, humidity and door state in control rooms and equipment cabinets; ICSA-26-260-06 for ABB Ability Edgenius, addressing CVE-2026-31431, a Linux kernel flaw where a locally authenticated user or a compromised container workload can escalate to root; and ICSA-26-260-07 for Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown, the agent that performs orderly shutdown of servers on UPS battery events. None is exploited. The Edgenius and PowerChute entries are the ones worth a second look, for different reasons. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 through ICSA-26-260-07 - Published 17 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA wants critical-infrastructure operators to plant tripwires — and to build them from tools they already own
item.category: Guidance — CISA, “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response”
item.description: CISA published guidance on deploying cyber decoys inside critical-infrastructure networks, aimed explicitly at teams that cannot detect an adversary using valid credentials and native administrative tooling. It describes three constructs: honeytokens, which are data elements or logical objects with no legitimate business purpose — fake records, credentials or files — whose use strongly implies unauthorised activity; breadcrumbs, planted references in scripts, documentation, file shares or configuration files that lead an intruder toward a monitored decoy; and honeypots, deliberately vulnerable systems. The instruction that makes this usable is the procurement one: repurpose existing EDR, identity and data-loss-prevention tooling to deploy and monitor decoys rather than buying a deception platform. The stated goal is reduced mean time to detection through high-fidelity alerts. - CISA guidance publication, reported by CyberScoop, Help Net Security and Industrial Cyber - Published 16 Sep 2026; sector coverage 17 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six agencies publish the seventeen ways attackers take Active Directory — which is how most of them reach a control network
item.category: Guidance — CISA, NSA and international partners on detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromise
item.description: CISA, the NSA and allied cyber agencies issued joint guidance cataloguing seventeen techniques used to compromise Active Directory, with detection and mitigation advice for each. The document is enterprise-focused, and that is precisely why it belongs on an OT page: in the overwhelming majority of industrial incidents, the path into the plant runs through the corporate directory. Engineering workstations joined to the corporate domain, HMI servers authenticating against it, jump hosts trusting it, and service accounts with rights on both sides are the standard architecture at most sites, and a compromised domain administrator inherits all of it. The techniques catalogued — Kerberoasting, unconstrained delegation abuse, AD certificate services misuse, DCSync and the rest — are the mechanics behind the phrase “no control systems were affected” in incident statements that nonetheless stopped production. - Joint guidance from CISA, the NSA and international partner agencies, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 16 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The substation risk assessment just got a method, a 36-month clock and a 1,500-foot neighbour test
item.category: Regulation — FERC order approving NERC Reliability Standard CIP-014-4; effective 1 October 2028
item.description: FERC issued an order on 10 September approving NERC Reliability Standard CIP-014-4, with the Federal Register notice published on 15 September and an effective date of 1 October 2028. The revisions target the part of CIP-014 that NERC concluded lacked rigour and consistency: the R1 risk assessment. Transmission owners must now identify applicable facilities existing or planned to be in service within a 36-month window, aligning the cycle with transmission planning; use a documented risk assessment methodology performing both steady-state and dynamic simulations on at least one system peak load case and one off-peak case; and identify proximate bulk electric system stations and substations within 1,500 feet, fence line to fence line, to evaluate the effect of an attack on adjacent equipment. It is a physical security standard, not a cyber one — but the assessment work, the ownership questions and the budget cycle all land on the same teams. - FERC order approving Reliability Standard CIP-014-4, Federal Register, reported by Industrial Cyber - FERC order 10 Sep 2026; Federal Register notice 15 Sep 2026; effective 1 Oct 2028 — verified 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The clock has started: anyone selling a connected product into the EU now owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
item.category: Regulation — EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations now in force
item.description: The reporting obligations under the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect on 11 September, with ENISA operating a Single Reporting Platform as the entry point. Manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must notify an actively exploited vulnerability within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, followed by fuller reporting, and must report severe incidents affecting product security on the same initial clock. For OT asset owners the direct obligation is limited — this falls on manufacturers — but the second-order effects are not. Expect more advisories, published faster, from vendors who previously disclosed quietly or not at all; expect procurement and legal teams to start asking vendors for CRA conformity evidence; and expect the vendors who cannot meet it to quietly stop selling certain legacy lines into Europe, which is a supportability question for anyone running them. - EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting commencement and the ENISA Single Reporting Platform, reported by Industrial Cyber - Reporting obligations effective 11 Sep 2026 — verified 18 Sep 2026
